g11-economics-ue5-t1.overview: Trade means buying, selling or exchanging goods and services, and it takes two broad forms: domestic trade within a country and international trade between countries. This lesson describes domestic and retail-wholesale trade, then explains why nations trade and how the WTO governs world trade.
objectives: Define trade and distinguish domestic trade from international trade
Compare retail trade and wholesale trade in the domestic market
Explain how domestic trade improves resource distribution and efficiency
Identify the immediate cause of trade among nations and the reasons for price differences
State the advantages of international trade and the role of the WTO
g11-economics-ue5-t1.simple: Trade is the buying, selling or exchanging of goods and services. Domestic trade happens inside one country; the market is limited by the country's borders. It has two parts: retail trade (selling goods directly to consumers, usually in small quantities) and wholesale trade (selling to other traders in bulk), which is the backbone of the domestic market. Domestic trade lowers transaction and transport costs, keeps money in the country and protects the economy from wars abroad, but it limits the choice of products. That limitation explains why all countries trade internationally. The immediate cause of international trade is the difference in prices of goods, caused by differences in resource endowments, technology and know-how. World trade today is administered by the World Trade Organization (WTO).
g11-economics-ue5-t1.detailed:
What trade is. Trade refers to the process of buying, selling or exchanging goods and services. There are two broad categories of trade: domestic trade and international trade. Domestic trade, also known as 'home trade', 'local trade' or 'internal trade', involves the flow of commodities by water, air and rail transport systems within a country or territory. Under domestic trade the market is constrained by the borders of that country, and all products must be bought and sold by people who live within the domestic market. International trade refers to the exchange of goods and services between two or more countries.

Retail and wholesale trade. Domestic trade can be further divided into retail trade and wholesale trade. Retail trade involves selling goods and services for direct consumption, while wholesale trade involves agents other than a standard consumer. Wholesale trade is the backbone of the domestic market. A retailer is normally the final seller of a product: it purchases from wholesalers and sells to the customers directly. Retailers have a credit arrangement with wholesalers and can repay after their sales are made in cash. Retailers sell goods in small quantities and are distributed all over the country where consumers live.

Why domestic trade matters. Historically, countries relied on domestic trade only, due to lack of skills, transportation and information. Domestic trade plays a crucial role in economic growth: by allowing different types of goods and services to reach all parts of the country, it improves the standard of living of residents and the employment rate. Domestic trade improves the economic performance of a country by improving resource distribution and efficiency. It also encourages investment and development within the country, eliminates dependence on foreign sources of goods, and makes the economy less exposed to political issues, international disagreements and wars. Countries with few manufacturing plants are likely to struggle during wartime because they have difficulty obtaining goods, services and equipment.

Benefits and limits of domestic trade. Domestic trade has several benefits over international trade. First, transaction costs associated with making sales tend to be much lower because there are no tariffs or customs duties. Second, transportation costs are much lower, and goods reach the market more quickly because of shorter distances. Through domestic trade a country keeps money within the country, which can finance future economic growth. However, the biggest limitation is the restricted selection of products available for sale: in pure domestic trade a country only trades what it produces, and some countries lack capacity and resources to meet their own demand. This is why today all countries engage in international trade to benefit from specialization and differences in endowments.

The basis of international trade. The immediate cause for trade among nations is the difference in the prices of goods and services. Prices differ because of differences in resource endowments, in the level of technology and in technical skills or know-how. For example, Ethiopia imports computers because it lacks the production technology, capital and know-how needed to make them; producing them at home would mean high costs and domestic prices above international prices, so residents prefer foreign computers. Nature has also distributed resources unevenly in the world, which makes production of some goods in some countries impossible. International trade therefore lets countries consume goods and services they could not produce themselves, such as coffee sold to Europe by Ethiopia.

The advantages of international trade. The textbook lists seven major advantages. It makes the most efficient use of world resources through specialization or the division of labor among nations. Each trading nation gains as world output increases, in the form of more aggregate production and a large number and greater diversity of quality goods. International trade relations help harmonize international political relations. Foreign competition induces efficiency in the home nation and maintains product quality. It helps domestic firms exploit economies of scale through expanding markets. It promotes learning through technology exchange, and cultural exchange and ties among countries develop through trade.

Who administers world trade. International trade is administered by the World Trade Organization (WTO), created on 1 January 1995. Before the WTO there was an arrangement called the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), which was the basis for countries to engage in international trade. From 1948 to 1994 the GATT provided the rules for much of world trade. Today the WTO is the only global international organization dealing with the rules of trade between nations: it is an organization for opening up trade, a forum for governments to negotiate trade agreements, and it operates a system of trade rules and facilitates the settlement of trade disputes among trading countries.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia desires computers, but producing them at home would require expensive capital and technology it lacks. Why does Ethiopia import computers instead of making them?
workedExamples.given: Ethiopia lacks the production technology, capital and know-how for computers, so domestic production costs are high.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the immediate cause of trade among nations is the difference in prices of goods and services; imports come in where foreign prices are lower.
workedExamples.substitution: If Ethiopia produced computers domestically, high production costs would give domestic prices above international prices.
workedExamples.calculation: Facing higher prices at home than abroad, domestic residents prefer foreign computers, so it is worthwhile to import computers cheaply rather than produce them at higher cost.
workedExamples.answer: Ethiopia imports computers because the country has an absolute disadvantage in making them; importing at lower international prices raises national welfare.

workedExamples.problem: In Dire Dawa a merchant buys cloth in very large quantities from a distributor using a credit arrangement and later resells it in small amounts to household consumers. Identify the two roles and the type of trade being performed.
workedExamples.given: The merchant buys in bulk from another trader on credit and resells in small quantities to final consumers.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: retail trade involves selling for direct consumption while wholesale trade involves agents other than a standard consumer.
workedExamples.substitution: Buying in bulk from a distributor is wholesale trade; selling in small quantities to consumers is retail trade.
workedExamples.calculation: The distributor is the wholesaler and the merchant is the retailer; the merchant receives credit from the wholesaler and repays after cash sales are made.
workedExamples.answer: The act of buying in bulk is wholesale trade and the resale to consumers is retail trade; the merchant performs the retailer's role, which is the final stage of domestic trade.

workedExamples.problem: A lightly industrialized country fears that a coming war will cut off its imports. Which channel of trade protects it, and which kind of country is most at risk?
workedExamples.given: War interrupts international shipping, and the country has a strong domestic market but few manufacturing plants.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: political issues, international disagreements and wars have less effect on the economy when a country has strong domestic trade.
workedExamples.substitution: Domestic trade keeps goods moving inside the borders even when foreign shipments stop.
workedExamples.calculation: Because domestic trade supplies goods independently of foreign sources, the economy keeps functioning; however, countries with few manufacturing plants still find it difficult to obtain goods, services and equipment during wartime.
workedExamples.answer: Strong domestic trade protects the economy better than reliance on imports, but a country with few plants can still struggle during a war.

Saying international trade exists only between rich and poor countries, when the immediate cause is the difference in prices of goods and services.
Thinking tariffs and customs duties apply to goods moving within one country, when they apply to trade between nations.
Assuming the WTO sets every national trade policy, when it is a forum for negotiation and dispute settlement among trading countries.

g11-economics-ue5-t2.overview: Three classical views explain why nations trade: mercantilism, Adam Smith's absolute advantage and David Ricardo's comparative advantage. This lesson develops each theory with its assumptions, the Ethiopia-China and Ethiopia-Germany numerical examples, and the criticisms of each.
objectives: Describe the mercantilists' view that national wealth depends on precious metals
State Adam Smith's principle of absolute advantage and its assumptions
Compute gains from trade under complete specialization using absolute advantage
Apply Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage using opportunity cost
Contrast mercantilism, absolute advantage and comparative advantage and their criticisms
g11-economics-ue5-t2.simple: Mercantilist writers in Europe between 1500 and 1800 believed a country's wealth lies in precious metals like gold, so they urged exports and discouraged imports, treating trade as a zero-sum game. Classical thinkers rejected this: wealth is productive capacity. Adam Smith (1776) showed trade is positive-sum: each country should export goods in which it has an absolute advantage, producing them at lower cost, and import the rest, as in Ethiopia's coffee versus China's cloth. With complete specialization world output rises and both countries gain. David Ricardo (1817) went further with comparative advantage: even if one country is more efficient in both goods, each should produce the good with the lower opportunity cost. Ethiopia makes wine more cheaply relative to cars; Germany makes cars; both gain from trade.
g11-economics-ue5-t2.detailed:
The Mercantilists' view. Mercantilists were a group of writers who appeared in Europe, especially in England, during the period 1500-1800, and also in Spain, France, Portugal and the Netherlands. They were concerned with nation building, that is how to make a nation powerful economically and politically. Their underlying belief was that a country's wealth is based on holdings of precious metals like gold, since such revenues raise domestic output and employment. To accumulate gold, a country should export more than it imports: exports are good because they generate revenue, while imports are bad because they imply payments to other countries. A favorable trade balance, a surplus of exports over imports, brings payments in gold and silver. The mercantilists therefore advocated government regulation of trade, including tariffs and quotas to minimize imports, and saw trade as a zero-sum game in which one country's gain is another's loss.

The classical answer. Classical thinkers refuted this view: a nation's wealth is reflected in its productive capacity, its ability to produce final goods and services, not in its holdings of precious metals. They also criticized the mercantilists' static view of the world economy. Adam Smith advocated a dynamic view in which both trading partners can simultaneously enjoy higher levels of consumption and production with free trade. Yet mercantilism has two modern features still visible today: it was highly nationalistic, putting the home nation first, which matches officials who say exports are good because they create jobs while imports are not good, and it favored regulation and planning of economic activity as a means of fostering the goals of the nation.

Smith's absolute advantage. Adam Smith (1723-1790), a Scottish philosopher and professor of Moral Philosophy at Glasgow, published 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' in 1776, attacking the mercantilists and advocating free trade. Using the analogy of a tailor who does not make his own shoes but exchanges a suit for shoes from a shoemaker, he argued that countries gain by concentrating on goods they can make most cheaply. The absolute cost advantage is the ability of one country to produce one of the two goods at a lower cost relative to its trading partner: Ethiopia produces coffee at a lower cost and sells it to European countries, while Germany and France have an absolute advantage in processed goods like machines and perfumes. Smith also advocated laissez faire, French for 'let people do as they choose', meaning economic affairs are best guided by the decisions of individuals, with government removing barriers to the market. For Smith trade is a positive-sum game, where all players can receive a positive return, not a zero-sum relationship.

Smith's model with Ethiopia and China. Smith's model assumes two countries and two goods, labor as the only homogeneous factor, the labor theory of value (the price of a good equals the labor time it contains), labor mobile within a country but immobile internationally, full employment, constant technology, zero transport costs, barter exchange and perfect competition. Table 5.1 of the textbook assumes Ethiopia and China each have 2 units of labor. Ethiopia produces 4 kgs of coffee per labor hour against China's 1 kg, while China produces 5 yards of cloth per labor hour against Ethiopia's 2 yards. Before trade, called autarky, total world output with 1 labor unit on each good is 5 kgs of coffee and 7 yards of cloth. If each country completely specializes, Ethiopia makes 8 kgs of coffee and China makes 10 yards of cloth. Exchanging 4 kgs of coffee for 4 yards of cloth at a 1:1 rate leaves Ethiopia consuming 4 kgs of coffee and 4 yards of cloth and China consuming 4 kgs of coffee and 6 yards of cloth, so total gains from specialization and trade equal 2 kgs of coffee and 4 yards of cloth, with the lion's share going to China due to the productivity difference and the assumed terms of trade. Both countries gain, proving trade is not zero-sum.

Limitations of Smith and Ricardo's breakthrough. Smith's theory has weaknesses: labor may not be the only factor and is not homogeneous across countries; absolute advantage explains only a small part of world trade, such as trade between developed and developing countries; and it cannot say what happens when one country has an absolute advantage in both goods. David Ricardo (1772-1823), a British economist famous for his theories of rent and comparative cost, formalized the principle of comparative advantage in his 1817 book 'The Principles of Political Economy and Taxation', using opportunity cost, defined as the next best alternative forgone. Ricardo's principle says mutually beneficial trade can take place even if one country has an absolute cost advantage in the production of both goods: the efficient nation should specialize in the good where its absolute advantage is greater, and the less efficient nation should specialize where its absolute disadvantage is smaller.

Ricardo's numerical example. Assuming Ethiopia and Germany produce automobiles and wine with labor hours of 100 (Ethiopia, car), 80 (Ethiopia, wine), 40 (Germany, car) and 60 (Germany, wine), Germany has an absolute advantage in both goods, so by Smith there would be no basis for trade. But the opportunity cost of 1 automobile is 1.25 wine in Ethiopia (100/80) and 0.67 wine in Germany (40/60), so Germany is relatively more efficient in cars. The opportunity cost of 1 wine is 0.8 cars in Ethiopia (80/100) and 1.5 cars in Germany (60/40). Ethiopia therefore has a comparative advantage in wine and Germany in automobiles, and mutually beneficial trade exists through the differences in opportunity costs. Ricardo's theory is criticized for assuming the labor theory of value with homogeneous labor, when labor is only one factor and is not homogeneous, and for assuming constant returns to scale and thus constant production costs in both nations.

workedExamples.problem: Using Smith's example, Ethiopia (2 units of labor, 4 kgs of coffee per labor hour, 2 yards of cloth) and China (2 units of labor, 1 kg of coffee, 5 yards of cloth) trade at an exchange rate of 1 kg of coffee for 1 yard of cloth, exchanging 4 units. Calculate the gains from trade.
workedExamples.given: Before trade world output is 5 kgs of coffee and 7 yards of cloth. Under complete specialization Ethiopia produces 8 kgs of coffee and China 10 yards of cloth.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: gains from trade equal world output after specialization and exchange minus output under autarky.
workedExamples.substitution: After specialization and exchanging 4 coffee for 4 cloth, Ethiopia consumes 4 coffee and 4 cloth; China consumes 4 coffee and 6 cloth.
workedExamples.calculation: Before trade each country split its 2 units of labor, producing 5 kgs of coffee and 7 yards of cloth in total. After specialization world output is 8 kgs of coffee and 10 yards of cloth. Exchanging 4 of Ethiopia's coffee for 4 of China's cloth leaves Ethiopia consuming 4 coffee and 4 cloth and China consuming 4 coffee and 6 cloth.
workedExamples.answer: Both countries consume more of at least one good than under autarky; the textbook reports total gains from specialization and trade of 2 kgs of coffee and 4 yards of cloth, with the lion's share going to China.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia needs 100 labor hours for 1 automobile and 80 hours for 1 unit of wine; Germany needs 40 hours for an automobile and 60 hours for a unit of wine. Which country has comparative advantage in which good?
workedExamples.given: Labor hours per unit: Ethiopia (car 100, wine 80); Germany (car 40, wine 60). Germany has absolute advantage in both goods.
workedExamples.formula: Opportunity cost of a car = hours per car / hours per wine; opportunity cost of wine = hours per wine / hours per car. Comparative advantage belongs to the lower opportunity cost.
workedExamples.substitution: Ethiopia: car = 100/80 = 1.25 wine; wine = 80/100 = 0.8 cars. Germany: car = 40/60 = 0.67 wine; wine = 60/40 = 1.5 cars.
workedExamples.calculation: Ethiopia's wine costs 0.8 cars against Germany's 1.5 cars, so Ethiopia's relative disadvantage is smaller in wine. Germany's car costs 0.67 wine against Ethiopia's 1.25 wine.
workedExamples.answer: Ethiopia has comparative advantage in wine; Germany has comparative advantage in automobiles, so mutually beneficial trade is possible even though Germany is more efficient in both goods.

workedExamples.problem: A trade official claims that every export is good and every import is bad because exports bring in gold, exactly as the mercantilists argued. What does modern trade theory answer?
workedExamples.given: The official echoes mercantilism, the 1500-1800 doctrine that wealth is measured in precious metals.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: classical thinkers refuted that wealth lies in precious metals; it is reflected in productive capacity, and trade is positive-sum rather than zero-sum.
workedExamples.substitution: If Ethiopia both exports coffee (Smith's absolute advantage) and imports machines at lower cost, both Ethiopia and its partners enjoy higher consumption.
workedExamples.calculation: Restricting all imports reduces efficiency, product diversity and technology exchange, so the classical view favors free trade with gains for both partners.
workedExamples.answer: Exports and imports can both benefit the country; national wealth depends on productive capacity, and trade is mutually beneficial, not a zero-sum game.

commonMistakes: Saying a country needs an absolute advantage in at least one good before trade can benefit it, which is Smith's theory but not Ricardo's.
Confusing mercantilism with free trade, when mercantilists advocated government regulation, tariffs and quotas to minimize imports.
Defining opportunity cost as the money price of a good instead of the next best alternative forgone.
Comparing absolute advantage using opportunity costs and comparative advantage using labor hours; the two measures belong to the two different theories.
Assuming trade is a zero-sum game and that imports must always be bad.
Forgetting that under specialization a country moves all its labor to the good in which it has the comparative advantage.
Ignoring the assumptions of the models, such as labor as the only factor, zero transport costs and barter trade.
applications: Ethiopia's coffee exports to Europe illustrate absolute advantage in a climate and skill Ethiopia has, while Europeans lead in machines and perfumes.
Judging the claim that exports create jobs and imports destroy jobs, a mercantilist argument still heard from public officials today.
Choosing to export goods whose domestic opportunity cost is low, such as coffee, and importing goods like computers that are expensive to produce at home.
Evaluating how a lesson from Ricardo supports Ethiopia importing technology rather than forcing costly local production of everything.
Explaining to a farmer that exchanging coffee for machinery can raise total consumption for both sides of the bargain.
g11-economics-ue5-t2.summary: Mercantilists (1500-1800) viewed wealth as holdings of precious metals and urged export surpluses through government regulation, treating trade as zero-sum; classical thinkers answered that wealth is productive capacity and trade can benefit everyone. Adam Smith's absolute advantage showed that specialization where cost is lowest raises world output, proven by the Ethiopia-China coffee-and-cloth example. Ricardo's comparative advantage went further: using opportunity cost, mutually beneficial trade exists even when one country is more efficient in both goods, as Ethiopia's wine and Germany's automobiles show.

g11-economics-ue5-t3.overview: A country's dealings with the world cover visible goods, invisible goods and finance, all recorded systematically in the balance of payments. This lesson defines the BoP, explains credit and debit items, and breaks down the current account, the capital account and how deficits are settled.
objectives: Define the balance of payments as a systematic record of transactions with the rest of the world
Classify BoP transactions as credit (inward payment) or debit (outward payment) items
Compute the current account balance from the trade balance, net services and net transfers
Distinguish the current account from the capital (financial) account
Explain how a current account deficit is financed through the capital account or official reserves
g11-economics-ue5-t3.simple: International trade means every country deals in three kinds of exchange: visible goods (physical goods exported and imported), invisible goods (services such as transport, education and medical services) and capital transfers (financial receipts and payments). All of these are recorded in the balance of payments, a systematic, double-entry record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a given period. Transactions that bring money in, such as exports, are credits recorded with a plus sign; transactions that send money out, such as imports, are debits recorded with a minus sign. The BoP has two main accounts: the current account, made up of the trade balance, net services and net transfers, and the capital account of financial flows. Overall, BoP equals the current account plus the capital account, and shortages are covered from foreign exchange reserves.
g11-economics-ue5-t3.detailed:
Three aspects of exchange and the BoP record. International trade implies a country has to deal with three aspects of exchange: transactions in visible goods, which include all types of physical goods exported and imported; invisible goods, meaning export and import of services such as transport, education and medical services; and capital transfers, which are concerned with financial receipts and payments. These transactions are recorded in the balance of payments (BoP), a systematic record of all economic transactions of a country with the rest of the world during a given period of time. It is a double entry system of record carried out in a specific period of time.

Credit and debit items. Any transaction in the BoP involves debit and credit items. Credit items reflect transactions that give rise to payments inward to the home country and are recorded with a plus sign: the main ones are exports, foreign direct investment inflow to the home country, and receipts of interest and dividends by the home country from earlier investment abroad. Debit items reflect transactions that give rise to payments outward from the home country and are recorded with a minus sign: imports, investments made in foreign countries by domestic nationals, and payments of interest and dividends by the home country on earlier investments made by foreign investors. The BoP is one of the most important economic indicators for policy makers because it shows how many goods and services the country exported and imported and whether it has been borrowing from or lending to the rest of the world.

The current account. There are two main accounts in the BoP: the current account and the capital account, sometimes called the financial account. The current account includes transactions in goods, services, investment incomes and current transfers, and records inflows and outflows of foreign currency from flows of goods, flows of services and unrequited (unilateral) transfers. It is composed of three balances. The trade balance shows the balance in the trading of merchandise goods, excluding trade in services, so it is narrower than the current account. When the value of exports is more than that of imports, the country has a trade surplus, a favorable or positive foreign trade; when import values exceed export values it has a trade deficit, an unfavorable or negative foreign trade; when the two are equal it is a trade balance. Net services is the difference between the export and import of services such as shipping, insurance and banking: ships must be hired to move goods, merchandise has to be insured against loss and damage in transit, and banking services facilitate receipts from and payments to foreign dealers. Net transfers are transactions like gifts, remittances and donations, which are unrequited or unilateral because residents receive them 'for free', with nothing paid in return at present or in the future. The current account balance is the sum of the trade balance, net services and net transfers during a given period.

The capital account. The capital account, broadly defined, includes transactions in financial instruments and central bank reserves. It records the movement of financial capital into and out of a country. Capital comes in through borrowing, sales of overseas assets and investments in a country by foreigners; these are capital inflows and are recorded as credits. Capital leaves through lending, buying of overseas assets, and purchases of domestic assets owned by foreign residents; these are capital outflows recorded as debits. The balance on capital account measures the outflow and inflow of funds for purchasing and selling assets abroad, and it may be positive (surplus) or negative (deficit).

The overall balance and how deficits are paid. Overall balance of payments is the sum of the current account balance (CA) and the capital account balance (KA): BoP = CA + KA. When a country is in current account deficit it must pay the difference between imports and exports from a surplus in the capital account. If there is no surplus, or the surplus is not enough to cover the current account deficit, the country pays the difference from the official reserve accounts, because the country needs to settle its bills; this is why countries sometimes have to restrict or control international trade flows. When receipts and payments are equal the BoP is in balance. If total BoP receipts exceed payments, the excess goes to the third account, the foreign exchange reserves; when payments exceed receipts there is a depletion of foreign exchange reserves.

g11-economics-ue5-t4.overview: Governments act to encourage or restrict international trade. This lesson defines trade policies, contrasts price restrictions (tariffs) with quantity restrictions (import quotas), lists the reasons for restricting trade, and explains the import substitution and export promotion strategies.
objectives: Define trade policies and distinguish encouraging from restrictive interventions
Explain how a tariff raises import prices and increases government revenue
Contrast price-related restrictions (tariffs) with quantity-related restrictions (quotas)
List the textbook reasons for restricting trade
Compare import substitution and export promotion as trade strategies
g11-economics-ue5-t4.simple: Trade policies are the actions and arrangements a country takes to encourage or restrict international trade; interventions that aim to discourage trade are called restrictive policies. Restrictions are broadly price-related or quantity-related. A tariff is a tax on imported goods, called custom duty or import duty, which raises the price of imports in the domestic market and so reduces demand for them, while also increasing government revenue. An import quota fixes the maximum quantity of a good that may be imported and allots this quantity to importers; nothing beyond it can enter. Governments restrict trade to protect jobs, protect infant industries, maintain the standard of living, equalize production costs, and for national security and cultural reasons. Two broad strategies guide trade: import substitution replaces imports with domestic production, and export promotion gives preferential support to the export sector to earn foreign currency.
g11-economics-ue5-t4.detailed:
What trade policies are. Trade policies refer to actions and arrangements that are taken by a country to encourage or restrict international trade. When the interventions aim to discourage international trade, the policies are 'restrictive policies'. Trade restriction is a policy introduced by countries on the trade of goods and/or services between two or more countries to limit the volume of trade and the associated transactions. Trade restrictions are imposed mainly on foreign trade, particularly on imports, and are broadly of two types: price-related and quantity-related restrictions.

Tariffs: restrictions by price. Tariff restrictions are taxes on the import of goods, called 'custom duty' or 'import duty'. Such taxes raise the price of imported goods in the domestic market. These higher prices are expected to reduce the demand for imports in the domestic market and thus act to restrict imports. Note that a tariff also increases government revenue, which is why tariff protection has a fiscal as well as a protective effect.

Quotas: restrictions by quantity. A quantitative restriction, the import quota, takes the shape of fixing the maximum quantity of goods permitted to be imported. The government determines the total import quota, that is the total amount of goods that can be imported, and allots this quota to various importers. Nothing beyond the quota can be imported, which naturally limits the quantity of imports. Unlike a tariff, a quota restricts trade by regulating the physical amount rather than by changing the price.

Why governments restrict trade. The textbook lists six reasons for restricting trade. It is done to protect domestic jobs, the job protection argument; to protect small and infant industries, the infant industry argument; to maintain the domestic standard of living; to equalize production costs with those of trading partners; for the purpose of national security; and for cultural and sociological considerations.

Import substitution (IS). Import substitution is a trade and economic policy that advocates replacing imports with domestic products, through special support packages to promote domestic producers. The idea of import substituting industrialization was popular in many developing countries from the early twentieth century until the late 1970s. The strategy was born due to lack of access to imports or a shortage of foreign currencies to pay for them. It has at least two important effects: infant or young industries are protected from competing with cheap imports through tariff barriers, quantitative restrictions and other measures, and the tariffs on imports help increase government revenue.

Export promotion (EP). Export promotion is the act of policy measures which actually or potentially enhance exporting activity at the company, industry or national level. The strategy gives preferential treatment to the export sector so as to generate revenue in foreign currency. This entails providing incentives over and above those which would prevail in a neutral strategy, for instance favoring exporters with credit, tax or exchange-rate arrangements. Note the difference in spirit: import substitution turns the economy inward to save foreign currency, while export promotion turns it outward to earn foreign currency.

workedExamples.problem: A government imposes a tax of customs duty on imported cloth, while in another case it announces that no more than 50,000 rolls of cloth may enter per year, split among licensed importers. Which restriction is price-related and which is quantity-related, and why?
workedExamples.given: Case 1: a customs duty on each roll. Case 2: a fixed maximum of 50,000 rolls per year allotted to importers.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: trade restrictions are price-related (changing the price of imports) or quantity-related (limiting the physical amount).
workedExamples.substitution: The customs duty raises the domestic price of imported cloth; the 50,000-roll ceiling caps the amount regardless of price.
workedExamples.calculation: A duty raises prices so consumers buy less, and the government collects revenue on what still arrives. A quota blocks anything beyond the fixed amount, so price plays no regulating role.
workedExamples.answer: Case 1 is a tariff, a price-related restriction; case 2 is an import quota, a quantity-related restriction.

workedExamples.problem: A new Ethiopian industry making processed coffee products cannot compete with cheap imported packaged coffee. Which restriction type and which reason for restriction fit this case?

workedExamples.substitution: A tariff or quota on imported packaged products raises their price or caps their volume while the young industry matures.
workedExamples.calculation: Using the infant industry argument, the government can protect the industry through tariff barriers and quantitative restrictions until it can compete; such tariffs also increase government revenue.

workedExamples.given: Country A supports domestic producers to replace imports; Country B gives incentives above those of a neutral strategy to exporters.

Tariffs are price-related restrictions that tax imports, raising their prices and government revenue; import quotas are quantity-related restrictions that cap the allowed volume. Governments restrict trade to protect jobs and infant industries, maintain living standards, equalize production costs and for security and cultural reasons, and countries choose between import substitution, which replaces imports with domestic production, and export promotion, which offers preferential support to exporters to earn foreign currency.

g11-economics-ue5-t5.overview: Currencies trade against each other in the foreign exchange market, where demand and supply set the exchange rate. This lesson explains nominal and real exchange rates with the burger example, and contrasts fixed and floating exchange rate systems, devaluation and revaluation, and appreciation and depreciation.
objectives: Define the foreign exchange market and the sources of demand for and supply of foreign currency
Define the nominal exchange rate and compute currency conversions
Compute the real exchange rate as the nominal rate times the ratio of foreign to domestic prices
Distinguish fixed from floating exchange rate systems including managed floating and NBE practice
Explain devaluation, revaluation, appreciation and depreciation and their effects on exports and imports
g11-economics-ue5-t5.simple: The foreign exchange (forex) market is the market that determines the exchange rate for global currencies, based on demand and supply of currencies. Demand for foreign currency comes from tourists, importers and investors abroad; supply comes from export earnings, tourist spending and foreign direct investment. The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another: at the time of writing, 1 USD costs close to 45 ETB, and 1 ETB buys about 0.022 USD. The nominal exchange rate states this price; the real exchange rate, equal to the nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of foreign to domestic prices, tells how many goods can be bought abroad relative to home, like the 5 dollar burger costing 60 birr. Under a fixed rate the government or national bank fixes the price, allowing devaluation or revaluation; under a floating rate the market sets the price, allowing appreciation and depreciation. Devaluation and depreciation make imports expensive and exports cheaper.
g11-economics-ue5-t5.detailed:
The foreign exchange market and the exchange rate. The foreign exchange market is a market place that determines the exchange rate for global currencies; it is sometimes called the 'forex market' or 'currency market', a place where the trading of one currency for another takes place, based on the interactions of demand and supply for currencies. The demand for foreign currencies arises from tourist visits to another country, import demand for goods from other nations, and demand to invest abroad. The supply of a nation's foreign currency arises from earnings such as tourist expenditure, export earnings and foreign direct investment. The exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another currency.

Nominal exchange rate. The nominal exchange rate is the rate at which currency can be exchanged for another: the number of units of the domestic currency that can purchase a unit of a given foreign currency. There are two ways of expressing it: the price of one unit of foreign currency in terms of domestic currency, or the price of one unit of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency. For example, at the time of going to press, Ethiopia buys 1 USD for close to 45 ETB, so the exchange rate for USD equals 45; the rate between the European Euro and the Ethiopian Birr is close to 53. Expressed the other way, 1 ETB buys just 0.022 USD. In most economic analysis the first definition, the domestic price of the foreign currency, is used. Nominal exchange rate is usually expressed as the domestic price of the foreign currency.

Real exchange rate. The real exchange rate tells us how many goods and services in the domestic country can be exchanged for the goods and services in a foreign country. Using the domestic currency required to buy one unit of foreign currency, the real exchange rate is the ratio of the price level abroad and the domestic price level, where the foreign price is converted into domestic currency units via the current nominal exchange rate. Symbolically, real exchange rate = e * (P*/P), where e is the nominal ETB-USD exchange rate, P* is the average price of a good in the foreign market and P the average price in Ethiopia. In the textbook example a burger costs 60 Birr in Addis Ababa and 5 USD in the USA: the foreign price converted into Birr is 45 x 5 = 225 Birr for one US burger, so the real exchange rate is 225/60 = 3.75: five USD will buy 3.75 more units of burger in Ethiopia than in the USA with the existing nominal rate and prices. If the price of the burger rises to 100 Birr due to, say, inflation, the real exchange rate becomes 225/100 = 2.25. If the real exchange rate equals 1, it costs the same amount of money to buy a given good in both countries.

Fixed exchange rate systems. A fixed exchange rate is a situation where the price of one currency in terms of another currency is fixed by a government or national bank. The exchange rate is determined by the national bank at the point where the demand for foreign currency equals its supply, made possible by intervening in the foreign exchange market through buying and selling of foreign currency, which requires monetary authorities to hold an inventory of foreign currency to supply in exchange for domestic currency. Advantages include stability of the value of the local currency, greater certainty for exporters and importers, and helping the government maintain low inflation. Under a fixed system a change in the exchange rate requires government or central bank intervention: devaluation refers to an increase in the foreign exchange rate (the local price of foreign currency rises), while revaluation is the opposite. Devaluation of a local currency is generally expected to encourage export earnings and discourage imports, since imports become expensive while exports become cheaper in the international market.

Floating exchange rate systems. A floating or flexible exchange rate is a regime where the price of the domestic currency is set by the foreign exchange market based on the interaction between supply and demand of the currencies; floating rates are more common in the real world. Floating does not mean countries never intervene: managed floating describes a government or central bank manipulating its currency's price to maintain a currency price favorable for international trade. The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) closely follows the determination of the exchange rate between the Ethiopian Birr and other foreign currencies in line with the managed floating system. Under a flexible regime, changes in the exchange rate are called appreciation and depreciation. Given the exchange rate as the price of 1 unit of foreign currency, appreciation refers to a decrease in the foreign exchange rate while depreciation is the opposite: if the USD-ETB rate rises from 45 to 50 the Birr has depreciated, and if it falls to 30 the Birr has appreciated.

keyTerms.def: The market, also called the forex or currency market, that determines the exchange rate for global currencies through currency trading.
The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
The rate at which one currency can be exchanged for another, usually expressed as the number of units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.
The rate telling how many domestic goods and services exchange for foreign goods and services, equal to the nominal rate times the foreign price divided by the domestic price (e x P*/P).
A system where the currency price is fixed by a government or national bank, maintained by buying and selling foreign currency.
Under a fixed system, devaluation raises the foreign exchange rate and revaluation lowers it, done by government decision.
A regime where the currency price is set by the foreign exchange market through supply and demand.
Under a floating system, appreciation is a fall in the foreign exchange rate (their currency buys less), depreciation is a rise (their currency buys more).
A floating arrangement in which a government or central bank still manipulates the currency's price to keep it favorable for international trade.

workedExamples.given: e = 45 ETB/USD; P* = 5 USD (price abroad, per USD burger); P = 60 Birr (price in Ethiopia, per Ethiopian burger).
workedExamples.formula: Real exchange rate = nominal exchange rate x (foreign price / domestic price), with the foreign price converted into domestic currency units.
workedExamples.substitution: Apply it step by step: foreign price converted into Birr is 45 x 5 = 225 Birr for one US burger; then form the ratio 225/60.

workedExamples.formula: RER = e x P*/P; the higher the domestic price, the lower the purchasing power of converted foreign money.
workedExamples.calculation: 225 divided by 100 equals 2.25.

workedExamples.problem: The USD-ETB exchange rate moves from 45 to 50 in one case, and falls from 45 to 30 in another. Name the movements and state the effect of the first case on exports and imports.
workedExamples.given: Case 1: rate rises 45 to 50. Case 2: rate falls 45 to 30. The exchange rate is measured as the price of 1 USD in Birr.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: expressed as the price of foreign currency, a rise in the rate is depreciation (or devaluation under a fixed system) and a fall is appreciation (or revaluation).
workedExamples.substitution: Case 1 raises the Birr price of a dollar, so the Birr buys fewer dollars; case 2 lets the Birr buy more.

g11-economics-ue5-t5.summary: The foreign exchange market sets the exchange rate, the price of one currency in terms of another, through the demand from tourists, importers and investors and the supply from exports, tourism and direct investment. The nominal rate states the price, exemplified by 45 ETB per USD, while the real exchange rate, the nominal rate times the foreign-to-domestic price ratio, compares purchasing power, as in the 3.75 burger example. Fixed rates are set by governments with devaluation and revaluation; floating rates are market-set, allowing depreciation and appreciation, and Ethiopia follows managed floating through the NBE.

g11-economics-ue5-t6.overview: Regional integration is the process by which two or more countries agree to cooperate toward peace, stability and wealth, moving from free trade areas to economic unions. This lesson covers its advantages and costs, the four types of integration, and globalization as experienced in Ethiopia.
objectives: Define regional (economic) integration and its purpose
State the three broad advantages and three costs of economic integration
Distinguish free trade areas, customs unions, common markets and economic unions
Define globalization and its main drivers
Assess the benefits and downsides of globalization in the Ethiopian context
g11-economics-ue5-t6.simple: Regional integration is the process by which two or more countries agree to cooperate and work together to achieve peace, stability and wealth. It reduces costs for consumers and producers and increases trade among members, based on written agreements. Its advantages are trade benefits, employment benefits and improved political cooperation; its costs are trade diversion, reduced employment and reduced national sovereignty. Integration deepens in stages: a free trade area (like NAFTA) removes barriers between members; a customs union adds a common trade policy against outsiders; a common market (like COMESA) also frees labor and capital; an economic union (like the EU) adopts common economic policies. Globalization is the increasing interdependence of world economies, populations and cultures, driven by cross-border trade, capital flows and technology. It brings markets, technology and growth but also loss of cultural identity and exploitation of workers.
g11-economics-ue5-t6.detailed:
What regional integration is. Regional integration is the process by which two or more countries agree to cooperate and work together to achieve peace, stability and wealth. It is an arrangement among countries to meet a pre-defined common goal, and it aims to reduce costs for both consumers and producers and to increase trade between the countries involved in the agreement; it is sometimes called 'economic integration'. The regional agreement is based on one or more written agreements describing the areas of cooperation in detail. There are different degrees of integration, the simplest being a free trade area and the final stage political integration.

Advantages of economic integration. Economic integration leads to three broad advantages for all member countries: trade benefits, employment benefits and improved political cooperation. It can reduce the costs of trade, improve the availability of goods and services and increase consumer purchasing power in member nations. On employment, trade liberalization leads to market expansion, technology sharing and cross-border investment, which tends to improve employment opportunities. Finally, stronger economic ties give member countries an incentive and a platform for political cooperation: members are expected to resolve conflicts peacefully, which leads to greater stability in the region.

Costs of economic integration. Integration may not be without cost. Trade diversion is the possibility of shifting trade from an efficient non-member country to a less efficient member country: due to the agreement, members might trade with members even though non-members could supply the good cheaper, inducing inefficiency in the system. Firm relocation is the second cost: firms may move their business to cheaper countries due to the opening of borders, leading to loss of jobs and unemployment in the high-cost member countries. Third, integration implies erosion of national sovereignty, since members typically must adhere to rules on trade, monetary and fiscal policies established by the management of the economic union external to any nation, which can create inconsistencies with pressing national issues and goals.

The four types of integration. A free trade area is the most basic form of economic cooperation, in which member countries remove all barriers to trade between themselves but remain free to independently determine their own trade policies with non-member nations; an example is the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). A customs union builds on the free trade area and restricts members to trade with non-member countries in a similar manner: barriers are removed between members, and members agree to use a common trade policy against non-members. A common market allows the creation of economically integrated markets between members: trade barriers including any restrictions on the movement of labor and capital are removed, and there is a common trade policy for non-members; its primary advantage for workers is that they no longer need a visa or work permit to work in another member country. An example is the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA). An economic union is the final stage of economic integration: countries enter an agreement to remove barriers to trade and adopt common economic policies; an example is the European Union (EU).

Globalization defined. Globalization refers to the increasing interdependence of world economies, population and cultures. Its main drivers are the growing scale of cross-border trade of commodities and services, the flow of international capital, and the wide and rapid spread of technologies; it reflects increased interconnectedness and interdependence of peoples and countries. Countries may enjoy access to new markets and technology, exposure to a new way of life and culture, and an improved standard of living. Globalization lets companies find lower-cost ways to produce their products, and it increases global competition, which drives prices down and creates a larger variety of choices for consumers; lowered costs help people in both developing and developed countries live better on less money.

Technology transfer and the Ethiopian experience. Globalization can imply substantial technological upgrading in developing countries through different channels: a developing country can implement embodied technological change (ETC) by purchasing secondhand capital goods from more industrialized countries, and a late starter can enjoy the 'last comer' benefit of jumping directly onto a relatively new technology. Globalization has affected the Ethiopian economy positively in recent years: Ethiopia has attracted world class investors and technologies, cities and urban life have substantially changed due to access to technology and information, the economy has registered a rapid growth rate over several years, and Addis Ababa has flourished as the capital city of the African continent as the headquarters of the Organization of African Union. The downsides include loss of cultural identity and exploitation of employees in foreign countries, which is also a problem in Ethiopia.

workedExamples.problem: A member of a customs union buys iron rods from a member country at a higher price than an efficient non-member could supply, because the agreement encourages internal trade. Which cost of integration is displayed and why?
workedExamples.given: Member supplier: higher price. Non-member supplier: cheaper; the agreement favors member trade.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: trade diversion is the possibility of shifting trade from an efficient non-member country to a less efficient member country.
workedExamples.substitution: The purchase moved from the cheapest supplier to the member supplier on grounds of membership, not price.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the agreement forces or encourages members to trade among themselves although non-members could supply more cheaply, inefficiency is introduced.
workedExamples.answer: Trade diversion: the union diverts trade to a less efficient member, inducing inefficiency in the system.

workedExamples.problem: Classify each arrangement: (a) two countries abolish tariffs between themselves but tax goods from outside according to their own separate policies; (b) several countries abolish internal barriers and set one common trade policy on outsiders; (c) the same bloc additionally lets workers live and work anywhere inside it without permits; (d) the bloc finally adopts common economic policies. Name each stage.
workedExamples.given: Arrangements (a)-(d) deepen step by step, ending with common economic policies.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the four stages of economic integration are free trade area, customs union, common market and economic union.
workedExamples.substitution: Match each feature: separate external policies = free trade area; common external policy = customs union; free labor and capital = common market; common economic policies = economic union.
workedExamples.calculation: Feature (a) matches the free trade area (NAFTA style); (b) the customs union; (c) the common market (COMESA style); (d) the economic union (EU style).
workedExamples.answer: (a) Free trade area; (b) customs union; (c) common market; (d) economic union.

workedExamples.problem: After joining a regional bloc, an Ethiopian firm buys secondhand machines from industrialized countries and later adopts the newest digital tracking technology at once. Which two globalization channels are illustrated?
workedExamples.given: Case 1: purchase of secondhand capital goods from more industrialized countries. Case 2: jumping directly to a relatively new technology as a late starter.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: globalization upgrades technology through embodied technological change (ETC) and the 'last comer' benefit.
workedExamples.substitution: Buying used machines embodies technology in the equipment itself; adopting new technology directly skips older generations.
workedExamples.calculation: Both channels are ways a developing country can implement substantial technological upgrading opened by globalization.
workedExamples.answer: Case 1 is embodied technological change (ETC); case 2 is the last comer benefit of jumping to new technology.

workedExamples.problem: One country lists integration gains: trade costs fall, jobs grow through market expansion, and members negotiate peacefully. Another complains that union rules on monetary and fiscal policy override national needs. Classify these statements.
workedExamples.given: Statement 1 lists trade, employment and political cooperation effects. Statement 2 complains about external rule-making.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: integration brings three broad advantages (trade, employment, political cooperation) and three costs (trade diversion, reduced employment, reduced sovereignty).
workedExamples.substitution: Statement 1 matches the advantage list; statement 2 concerns adherence to union-set rules on trade, monetary and fiscal policies.
workedExamples.calculation: Rule-making by the management of the economic union, external to any nation, creates inconsistencies with pressing national issues and goals, which is the sovereignty cost.
workedExamples.answer: Statement 1 states the advantages of economic integration; statement 2 states the cost of reduced national sovereignty.

commonMistakes: Thinking a customs union and a free trade area are the same, when only the customs union sets a common trade policy against non-members.
Assuming integration only has benefits, when trade diversion, reduced employment and reduced sovereignty are real costs.
Calling trade diversion a benefit, when it shifts trade from efficient non-members to less efficient members and induces inefficiency.
Placing common-market privileges like visa-free work in a mere free trade area; free movement of labor belongs to the common market stage.
Mixing up the examples: NAFTA illustrates a free trade area, COMESA a common market and the EU an economic union.
Defining globalization as only more trade, when it also involves flows of international capital and rapid spread of technologies.
Overlooking that globalization has downsides, such as loss of cultural identity and exploitation of employees.
applications: Ethiopia's participation in regional blocs of the COMESA type illustrates how a common market arrangement covers Eastern and Southern Africa.
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which Ethiopia signed, applies the free trade area idea across the continent, as does regional cooperation among Horn of Africa neighbors.
United States trade preferences of the AGOA type for Ethiopian garments show how preferential agreements open member markets and raise exports.
Cooperation with international financial institutions such as IMF and the World Bank supports Ethiopia's trade financing and balance of payments management.
Globalization is visible in Ethiopia through foreign investors, technology access, and Addis Ababa as the seat of the African Union.
Discussing the loss of cultural identity and exploitation of workers as real downsides Ethiopia has experienced from globalization.

Its advantages are trade benefits, employment benefits and improved political cooperation, while its costs are trade diversion, reduced employment and reduced national sovereignty. Integration deepens through free trade areas, customs unions, common markets and economic unions, and globalization, driven by cross-border trade, capital and technology flows, has brought Ethiopia growth, investors and technology together with cultural and labor downsides.
